summary: p-limit is a small ESM library that wraps promise-returning functions so no more than a configured number run at once.
The single runtime module is index.js, which exports a default pLimit factory and a named limitFunction helper.
Each pLimit call builds a closure holding an active count, a concurrency value, and a FIFO queue from the yocto-queue dependency.
Calling the returned limit function enqueues the work and, when under the limit, dequeues and starts it; completion decrements the active count and starts the next queued item.
The returned function also exposes activeCount, pendingCount, clearQueue, a mutable concurrency property, and a map helper.
Tests live in test.js (AVA) and index.test-d.ts (tsd), benchmarks in benchmark.js using scripts/benchmarker.js, and CI runs npm test on Node 20/22/24.

interview.pitch: I am a tiny concurrency limiter for promise-returning functions. You call pLimit with a cap, get back a limit function, and every call you make through it only runs up to that many at once; the rest queue in a yocto-queue FIFO. It also ships limitFunction for wrapping one function, a map helper, active and pending counts, clearQueue, and a mutable concurrency setter, with full TypeScript types.
tradeoffs: All state is closure-scoped per limiter instance, so there is no global coordination across limiters.
clearQueue by default leaves pending promises unresolved unless rejectOnClear is enabled, which can hang awaiters.
Calling the same limiter recursively from within a limited task can deadlock because inner tasks queue behind themselves.
Concurrency is validated only at construction and on assignment, and setting it schedules resume via queueMicrotask rather than synchronously.

questions.q: How does p-limit preserve async execution context for queued tasks?
questions.a: enqueue wraps the run in a new Promise whose internal resolve is stored as queueItem.run; dequeue().run() then invokes run bound with the function, resolver, and arguments, preserving the caller's async context.

questions.q: Why resolve the caller promise before the function finishes?
questions.a: run calls resolve(result) immediately after creating the async IIFE, so callers get the underlying promise right away while the limiter awaits completion internally to track activeCount.

questions.q: What happens when the iterable throws inside limit.map?
questions.a: map catches the error, attaches catch handlers to already scheduled promises to avoid unhandled rejections, then rethrows the original error.
Without rejectOnClear it calls queue.clear(); with rejectOnClear it dequeues each pending item and rejects it with AbortSignal.abort().reason.

questions.q: What external dependency does p-limit rely on?
questions.a: It depends on yocto-queue for the FIFO queue, imported as the default Queue in index.js.

questions.q: How can concurrency be changed at runtime?
questions.a: The concurrency property setter validates the new value, updates the closed-over concurrency, and schedules a microtask that resumes queued tasks while activeCount is below the new limit.

# sindresorhus/p-limit

## Purpose
p-limit is a small ESM concurrency limiter for promise-returning functions. It wraps calls so no more than a configured number run at once, queueing the rest in a FIFO queue.

## Module map
| Module | Path | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| p-limit core | `.` | Factory and limiter implementation in `index.js` |
| Type definitions | `.` | TypeScript declarations in `index.d.ts` |
| Unit tests | `.` | AVA suite in `test.js` |
| Type tests | `.` | tsd assertions in `index.test-d.ts` |
| Benchmark script | `.` | Concurrency scenarios in `benchmark.js` |
| Benchmarker harness | `scripts` | Custom benchmark runner in `scripts/benchmarker.js` |
| CI workflow | `.github/workflows` | GitHub Actions test matrix in `.github/workflows/main.yml` |

## Request path
1. Caller invokes `pLimit(concurrency)` to obtain a limit function.
2. Calling `limit(fn, ...args)` creates a Promise and enqueues the task.
3. If `activeCount` is below concurrency, `resumeNext` dequeues and starts the task.
4. `run` executes the function in an async IIFE and resolves the caller promise immediately.
5. After the function settles, `next` decrements `activeCount` and calls `resumeNext`.
6. The queued caller promise resolves with the function result.

## Rules
- New runtime scheduling code belongs in `index.js`; new public type changes belong in `index.d.ts`.
- `core` owns concurrency state, queueing, execution, and runtime mutations.
- `types` owns TypeScript declarations only and must not implement runtime behavior.
- `tests` and `typetests` validate `core` but do not own production decisions.
- `benchmark` and `benchmarker` own performance scenarios and harness behavior, not limiter semantics.
- `ci` owns test execution across Node versions, not application logic.
- `core` should not import tests, type tests, benchmark code, or CI configuration.
- Non-core modules may depend on `core`; `benchmark` also depends on `benchmarker`.

## External services
- `yocto-queue`: FIFO queue dependency, owned by `core` through its import in `index.js`.

## Known weak spots
- `clearQueue()` leaves pending promises unresolved unless `rejectOnClear` is enabled.
- A limited task that calls the same limiter recursively can deadlock because inner tasks queue behind themselves.
- Changing `concurrency` validates and updates state, then schedules resumption with `queueMicrotask` rather than synchronously.
- Each limiter keeps closure-scoped state, so there is no coordination across separate limiter instances.
- Repeated calls enqueue separate tasks; there is no deduplication or idempotency layer.
